story_text.value:
I built this because it was useful for me when building evals/benchmarks, and I decided to put it up for free for others. The goal was quite simple, make it easy to use a lead claude code / codex session in a panel on the side, while allowing every cell to also be a terminal session running claude/codex, and make it possible to continue a session in an actual terminal window if I needed to. They can all talk to each other using cells on the grid, named cells, or the MCP server that effectively glues the app together. I also found it useful for managing context within related but disparate sessions.

My real benchmark runs with recalc are internal to my startup, so to demonstrate some of the functionality I built a small FDA Bench with the tool (obtain and put together dossier's of FDA submissions, and see if a harnessed Claude could have accurately predicted pass/fail): https://github.com/sshah03/recalc#a-model-benchmark

It is still very much a work in progress, but given the versatility of spreadsheet apps, wanted to see how others see themselves using it and what doesn't exist that would be useful to them. Currently runs locally on macs, linux as well but that's less tested, and Windows hasn't been tested at all so that'll come in the future.

story_text.value:
Hi, here's a TUI we originally created for internal use. The goal is to be able to control multiple Claude Code sessions running in parallel while being able to review the changes and to understand the design choices the agents make.

The key design principles are:

- the programmer's attention is the bottleneck, so instead of cycling between sessions to find what's waiting for user input we use hooks to push work to the attention queue, i.e. let work come to you, not viceversa

- easy change, review and comment loop: [tuicr](https://tuicr.dev/}-inspired code reviews. Easy to add comments and send them to agents

- unobtrusive tooling: run on tmux sessions, connect to claude code via hooks, no complex dependencies

- quiz mode: answer design questions about the code to verify and reinforce your understanding of the changes

- keyboard-first navigation with vim keybindings

Comments, ideas and PRs all welcome!

story_text.value:
The fastest way to learn harness engineering? Build Claude Code from scratch.

Why harness engineering? LangChain kept the same model and changed only the harness. Their coding agent went from 53% to 67% on Terminal-Bench, a top coding-agent benchmark. From outside the top 30 to the top 5. Same model. Better harness.

Over the past few months, I've taken apart Claude Code, OpenCode, and Pi to see how they work under the hood.

And you don't need to ship a coding agent for this to pay off. The same foundations power any agent, in e-commerce, finance, or sales.

On top of that, people are increasingly realizing they need to build their own harness instead of relying on Claude Code or Codex. Ramp scaling its operations with a custom harness is a perfect example.

So I turned what I learned into an in-depth course on harness engineering by building Claude Code from scratch. It's free and open source: 8 articles, 6 videos, and one codebase. It's perfect for people who learn by building. Everything in Python.

For full transparency, Modal, Opik, and Kitaru sponsor the course, which lets me keep it 100% free as an independent AI engineer.

Here are the 8 steps that I think are core to building and maintaining any harness:

1. Design the harness 2. Build the bare-bones agent loop 3. Sandbox it, locally and remotely 4. Apply 4 essential context engineering techniques 5. Add subagents as a context engineering technique 6. Deploy it headless to the cloud: CLI, webhooks, cron 7. Build benchmarks to measure it 8. Replay failed runs to debug agents

Everything is on GitHub: https://github.com/decodingai-magazine/building-a-coding-agent-from-scratch-course

Curious what others here think. Which of these steps has been the hardest to get right in your own agents?

story_text.value:
I build websites for a living. Lately, it's more about prompting than actually writing the code (the art part is still there). So I decided to leave that part to Claude too and see what it would come up with. So far, I have given it

- A baseline website - Full access to Google, X, LinkedIn and Reddit Ads, with a budget - Apify access - Openrouter access

I also wanted it to personalize the website completely based on the user. No 2 users see the same website, most of the content is rendered on the client side using Deepseek. It uses - Device (GPU model, battery percentage, fonts installed, resolution, adblock installed, camera and mic connected, mouse polling rate, scroll speed, etc) - Demographics (Weather, time of the day, news around you, ..) - Behavior (Scroll speed, clicks, selection, referrer, etc) - Tons of other connected services through Apify

So far it's doing tomfoolery for the most part. Like creating a gazzilion pages for SEO (exactly what our interns say every time), trying to go viral by adding share buttons, etc. But it's still super fun to see it make decisions every 4 hours.

title.value: Show HN: Just gave Claude Code the website and ad budget to see what it would do
